translation: Sanjaya said: To him who was thus overcome by pity, despondent, and whose eyes were blurred with tears, Madhusudana (Krishna) spoke these words.
The Blessed Lord said: O Arjuna! How has this dejection, which is unbefitting a noble person (Anarya-justam), which bars heaven, and causes disgrace, overtaken you at this critical juncture?
simple_explanation: Noble minds are guided by three restraints: self-reproach, fear of divine law, and public shame. This conduct lacks all three—it is anaryajusta (free from self-reproach), asvargya (defying divine law), and akirtikara (inviting public infamy). How could this inappropriate stupor cloud you on the field?

translation: O Partha! Do not yield to unmanliness; it does not become you. O scorcher of foes (Parantapa)! Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise!
Arjuna said: O Madhusudana! O destroyer of enemies! How can I counter-attack with arrows in battle Bhishma and Drona, who are worthy of my deepest worship?
It would be better to live on alms in this world than to slay these noble elders. If I kill them, all my enjoyments of wealth and desires in this world will be stained with their blood.
We do not even know which is better for us—that we conquer them or that they conquer us. The very sons of Dhritarashtra, after killing whom we would not care to live, stand arrayed before us.

With my natural Kshatriya disposition paralyzed by the taint of helplessness, and my mind confused regarding my duty (Dharma), I ask You: tell me decisively what is better for me. I am Your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in You.
For I do not see what can dispel this grief which dries up my senses, even if I should obtain an unrivaled, prosperous kingdom on earth or lordship over the celestial gods.
Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha, Gudakesha (Arjuna), the terror of foes, said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and fell silent.
O Dhritarashtra! Right between the two armies, Hrishikesha, smiling as it were, spoke these words to the despondent Arjuna.
The Blessed Lord said: You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom. The truly wise (Panditah) grieve neither for the dead nor for the living.
simple_explanation: You are displaying intellectual vanity, trying to justify an error with sophisticated arguments. Wise people do not grieve for the dead, for they are gone; nor do they grieve for the living, for they are too busy performing their duties to waste time on grief.

translation: Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these kings; nor shall any of us cease to exist hereafter. The individual soul is eternal; only its physical shell is temporary.

Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this physical body, it similarly transitions into another body after death. A self-controlled, serene person (Dhira) is not deluded by this.
O son of Kunti! The contacts of the senses with their objects (matra-sparsah), which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are transient and fleeting. Endure them patiently, O Bharata.
O foremost among men! That wise person who remains unagitated by these sense contacts, and stays equal in both pleasure and pain, becomes fit for immortality (Amritatva).
simple_explanation: As stated in Shatapatha Brahmana (2.2.2.14), immortality means achieving a full, undivided span of useful life, unbowed by adversaries. Senses will inevitably strike the body and age it, but remaining mentally equanimous amidst this wear and tear is true spiritual practice.

translation: The unreal (Asat) has no independent existence, and the real (Sat) never ceases to be. The ultimate truth concerning both has been perceived by the seers of essential truth (Tattvadarshibhih).
Know that to be imperishable by which this entire universe is pervaded. No one can bring about the destruction of this immutable principle.
These bodies are temporary, but the embodied soul (Sharirin) is eternal, indestructible, and boundless. Therefore, fight, O Bharata!
He who thinks that the soul kills, and he who thinks the soul is killed, both are ignorant. The soul neither kills nor is it killed.

The soul is never born, nor does it ever die; it does not come into being at some point and then cease to exist. It is unborn, eternal, permanent, and ancient; it is not destroyed when the body is destroyed. Grieving for it is like crying over a discarded coconut shell.
O Partha! He who knows this soul to be indestructible, eternal, unborn, and immutable—how can that person kill anyone, or cause anyone to be killed?
Just as a person casts off worn-out garments and puts on new ones, the embodied soul similarly leaves worn-out bodies and enters new ones.
simple_explanation: Consider this, Arjuna: does anyone weep when changing into new clothes? If a thief breaks into a house, steals pennies, but leaves a chest of diamonds safe, should the owner celebrate the diamonds or cry over the pennies? In this war, the true owner—the Soul—loses nothing.

translation: Weapons cannot cut this soul, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, and wind cannot dry it.
It is uncuttable, unburnable, insoluble, and undryable. It is everlasting, all-pervading, stable, unmoving, and ancient.
The soul is described as unmanifest, inconceivable, and immutable. Knowing it as such, you should not grieve over the body.
And even if you assume the soul to be constantly born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, you have no reason to grieve.
Death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who dies. Therefore, you should not grieve over this inevitable fact.
O Bharata! All created beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their interim state, and unmanifest again after death. What is there to lament?

Someone beholds this soul as a marvel, another speaks of it as a marvel, and someone else hears of it as a marvel. Yet, even after hearing about it, no one fully understands it. Do not let wonder turn into grief.
The embodied soul residing within the body of everyone is eternally immune to slaughter, O Bharata. Therefore, you should not mourn for any living creature.
simple_explanation: Arjuna's breakdown has two roots: misunderstanding Kshatriya duty and fearing the death of kinsmen. Krishna reduces the status of death to a mere change of clothes. He reveals: "Arjuna, your fundamental delusion is that a Kshatriya’s duty is svajana-raksha (protecting kinsmen). A Kshatriya looks neither at numbers nor at blood ties; a tyrant can never be a kinsman. Your duty is sujana-raksha (protecting the righteous). Every evil person is an enemy; every righteous person is a kinsman. Manu Smriti states: 'Slay a tyrant without hesitation, whether he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin.' This rule comes from Rigveda (4.26.2), where God says, 'I gave land to the Aryas (righteous),' not to one's kinsmen. Thus, your stance is anaryajusta."

translation: Moreover, considering your own specific duty (Svadharma), you should not waver; for there is nothing more meritorious for a Kshatriya than a righteous war.
O Partha! Happy and fortunate are the Kshatriyas who obtain unsolicited such an opportunity for war, which comes like an open gateway to heaven.
But if you do not wage this righteous war, you will fail in your duty, lose your reputation, and incur only sin.
simple_explanation: If a Kshatriya dies fighting for an unjust cause, he misses Svadharma but retains martial glory. If he runs away claiming the cause is unjust, he is accused of cowardice. But one who fights a righteous war gains both duty and glory.

translation: People will speak of your perpetual infamy for ages to come; and for a highly respected person, infamy is worse than death.
The great chariot-warriors will think you fled from battle out of fear; and you will be look down upon by those who held you in high esteem.
Your enemies will slander your capability and speak many unspeakable words. What could be more painful than that?
If you are killed, you will gain a higher, noble rebirth; if you conquer, you will enjoy the sovereignty of the earth. Therefore, arise, O son of Kunti, resolved to fight!
Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, prepare yourself for battle. Fighting thus, you shall never incur sin.
simple_explanation: As long as you calculate personal happiness, wealth, or victory, selfishness will stain your actions. When you act solely to defend justice, sin cannot touch you. To grasp the subsequent verses, we must define Sankhya and Yoga. Formulating a precise, structured definition of an ideal state is Sankhya. Prescribing the practical means to reach that state is Yoga. For instance, defining a mind free from anger is Sankhya; practicing meditation and austerity to achieve it is Yoga. The objective state is described in Sankhya, its attainment is executed via Yoga. They are interdependent.

translation: The wisdom presented to you so far belongs to the framework of Sankhya (analytical knowledge). Now hear the wisdom of Yoga (selfless action), equipped with which, O Partha, you will break free from the shackles of karma.
simple_explanation: Sankhya reveals the ideal: remaining unaffected by pleasure and pain. Yoga provides the method to cultivate this mind. This brings action without bondage. If a teacher spends extra time with a favored student due to personal attachment, his teaching becomes a binding action. If he gives exactly what is required without bias, he practices Karmayoga. Arjuna came to punish tyrants, but personal attachments blocked his path. Krishna rectifies this, but the literal ritualists (Vedavadah) stand in the way. Their misconceptions must be dispelled first. The True Veda vs. Ritualism: The Veda teaches surrender to God and public welfare. Later, greedy or lazy individuals turned these sacrifices into superstitious magic. To correct this, Vyasa wrote the Vedanta Sutras, and Jaimini wrote the Mimamsa. Combined, they define duty and its ultimate goal, God. However, medieval ritualists separated them. For example, the ancient text prescribed a "donkey sacrifice" (gardabhesti) as a penance for a fallen student—meaning he should live on simple food and work hard like a donkey to regain self- control. Medieval ritualists distorted this into slaughtering a literal donkey at a crossroads! They replaced "the character of animals" (pashunam rupam) with literal meat. These are the Vedavadah—exploiters of ritual who promise villages, wealth, or heaven for chanting formulas.

translation: In this path of selfless action, no effort is wasted, and there is no risk of counterproductive results. Even a tiny practice of this righteous path protects one from great fear.
O joy of the Kurus! The resolute, single-minded intellect (vyavasayatmika buddhi) focused on duty is one; but the thoughts of the irresolute sprout into endless, multi-branched desires.
O Partha! The unwise, who delight in the literal word of the Vedas and proclaim "there is nothing else beyond this," speak flowery words.
Driven by desires, viewing heaven as their supreme goal, they prescribe multi-layered, intricate rituals that lead to wealth, power, and rebirth as the reward for action.
The single-minded intellect focused on duty is never formed in the minds of those who are deeply attached to pleasure and power, and whose discrimination is stolen by that flowery speech.

The ritual texts deal with the modifications of the three qualities of nature (Gunas). Rise above these three attributes, O Arjuna! Free yourself from dualities, establish yourself firmly in pure goodness (Sattva), look beyond personal acquisition and preservation (yoga-kshema), and be anchored in the Self.
simple_explanation: Even a good quality can become a binding attachment. Studying scripture is a good quality, but if a guard on night duty forgets his post to study text, his attachment destroys the nation. Rise above attachments. This leaves you nirdvandva—unshaken by heat, cold, honor, or insult.

translation: To an enlightened person who knows the Truth, all the literal rituals of the Vedas hold as much utility as a tiny well when the entire land is flooded with water from all sides (samplutodake).
Your choice is over your action alone, never over its fruits. Do not let the fruits of action be your motive, nor let yourself be attached to inaction (Akarmani).
simple_explanation: This verse summarizes the core of Vedanta. An action that harms public welfare is Akarma (inaction/bad action); never lean toward it. When performing a good action, its execution is within your control, but its ultimate outcome rests with the Cosmic Law. This verse condemns attachment to the secondary rewards of fruit (phala-phala), not the goal itself. A doctor must ensure his medicine cures the disease, but he must not let his passion be driven by the fee he receives.

translation: Established in Yoga, perform actions, O Dhananjaya, casting off attachment and remaining equanimous in both success and failure. Equanimity of mind is called Yoga (Samatvam yoga uchyate).

Motivated, reward-seeking action is far inferior to the Yoga of wisdom, O Dhananjaya. Take refuge in selfless wisdom; those who are motivated solely by the rewards of action are wretched and small-minded (kripanah).
Endowed with equanimity, a person casts off both good and bad deeds in this life. Therefore, strive for this Yoga; excellence and skill in actions is Yoga (Yogah karmasu kaushalam).
simple_explanation: Renouncing attachment to a good deed is harder than renouncing a bad one. If Vibhishana had been attached to family loyalty (a conventional good deed), he could not have stood for global welfare. Skill in action means identifying which action serves the greater good, even if it appears unconventional.

translation: The wise, possessed of a balanced intellect, renouncing the fruits born of action, free themselves forever from the shackles of rebirth and attain that state which is free from all suffering (Anamayam padam).
When your intellect crosses beyond the mire of delusion, you will achieve complete indifference (Nirvedam) toward what has been heard and what is yet to be heard from ritual texts.

When your intellect, currently perplexed by conflicting ritual interpretations (shruti- vipratipanna), stands unshakable and unmoved in contemplation of the Divine, then you will attain the state of perfect Yoga.
simple_explanation: Yoga is not merely sitting in a corner holding one's breath. When a warrior, a merchant, or a laborer becomes single-mindedly absorbed in his duty, he is a Yogi. Rigveda (10.66.8) states that warriors who view justice as their sacrifice form the army of Indra. When your focus settles on Kshatriya duty, you attain state-equilibrium.

translation: Arjuna said: O Keshava! What are the defining characteristics of a person of steady wisdom (Sthitaprajna) who is anchored in contemplation? How does a person of stable mind speak, how does he sit, and how does he walk?

The Blessed Lord said: O Partha! When a person completely casts off all desires of the mind, and remains satisfied in the Self by the Self alone, then he is called a person of steady wisdom (Sthitaprajna).
He whose mind remains unagitated amidst miseries, who is free from longing amidst pleasures, and from whom attachment, fear, and anger have departed, is called a sage of steady mind (Sthitadhih).
He who is without attachment on all sides, and who neither rejoices upon obtaining good nor gets dejected upon encountering evil—his wisdom is firmly established.

And when a person completely withdraws his senses from their objects, just as a tortoise pulls its limbs into its shell, his wisdom is firmly established. This is called Pratyahara in Yoga philosophy.
Senses recede from an abstinent embodied soul, leaving behind only the subtle longing (rasa). But even this subtle longing fades away when the supreme truth is directly perceived.
O son of Kunti! The turbulent senses violently carry away the mind of even a wise person who is striving to control them.

Restraining all of them, a disciplined person should sit focused on Me as the ultimate goal. For he whose senses are completely under control—his wisdom is firmly established. Follow my example, as I am anchored in the Divine.
Dwelling on the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment to them. From attachment arises longing desire (Kama), and from unfulfilled desire springs anger (Krodha).

From anger arises delusion, from delusion comes loss of memory, from loss of memory comes the ruin of discrimination (Buddhi), and with the ruin of discrimination, the human being is utterly destroyed.
But a self-controlled practitioner, moving among sense objects with senses free from attraction and aversion, and fully submissive to the Self, attains inner tranquility (Prasada).
simple_explanation: Senses interacting with objects is not a flaw; it is the source of all empirical knowledge. But when attraction or aversion stains this perception, vision gets clouded. Just as a fool might burn priceless manuscripts to boil water due to his blinding need for fuel, an attached mind loses its sense of value. Arjuna’s attachment to blood ties has blinded him to Duryodhana’s crimes.

translation: With the attainment of inner tranquility, all his miseries are completely obliterated. The intellect of such a serene person quickly becomes steady and well-established.
An undisciplined person lacks resolute wisdom, and he can have no depth of meditation. To one without meditation, there is no peace; and to the unpeaceful, how can there be happiness?
For the mind that follows the wandering senses carries away a person's wisdom, just as a fierce wind sweeps away a rudderless boat upon the waters.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, he whose senses are completely shielded from their respective objects possesses firmly established wisdom.

What is night for all living beings is the time of awakening for the self-controlled person; and the state of ephemeral consciousness in which all beings keep awake is night for the see-er of Truth (Muni).
simple_explanation: Ordinary individuals dose off the moment the word "duty" is uttered, but snap awake for sensual updates. The world of higher duty is a dark night to the worldly, but the self- controlled person thrives in it.

translation: Just as the ocean remains undisturbed and stable within its deep boundaries though filled incessantly by rivers pouring into it from all sides, a person into whom all objective desires enter without causing a ripple attains peace—never the path-seeker of desires (kama-kami).
That person who, abandoning all desires, moves through life free from longing, free from the sense of ownership (Nirmamah), and free from egoism (Nirahankarah), attains ultimate peace.

O Partha! This is the state of resting in the Divine (Brahmi sthitih). Attaining this, a person is never deluded again. Established in this state even at the hour of death, one attains liberation into the absolute peace of Brahman (Brahma-nirvanam).
